title: Supreme Court wants affidavit on IPS postings in CAPFs, continues oversight of 2025 judgment
author: Vijaita Singh
content_html:
The Supreme Court’s order in the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPF) cadre case, uploaded on Saturday (September 5, 2026), specifically asks Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan to explain the procedure followed for bringing Indian Police Service (IPS) officers on deputation to the CAPFs, including whether the borrowing organisations had made formal requisitions, and the reasons for making such appointments despite the court’s earlier direction to progressively reduce IPS deputation posts up to the Senior Administrative Grade level. The court said that it “shall continue monitoring of implementation of the judgment” dated May 23, 2025.

On September 2, while hearing a contempt petition filed by former CAPF officers regarding the non-implementation of the top court’s 2025 order to progressively reduce IPS deputation in CAPFs up to the rank of Inspector Generals in the next two years, the court had sought an explanation from Mr. Mohan.

‘Strong lobby’

Justice Ujjal Bhuyan had orally observed that there was a “strong lobby” and the cadre officers of CAPFs were completely stifled.

On Saturday (September 5), the order uploaded by the Bench of Justice Ujjal Bhuyan and Justice Atul S. Chandurkar, said: “Before we pass necessary order(s), we direct the Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Home Affairs to explain the above statement, for bringing in IPS officers on deputation to the five CAPFs; what procedure was followed before bringing the above officers on deputation i.e., whether any requisition was made by the borrowing department for deputation etc. and the reasons for bringing them on deputation notwithstanding the judgment of this court directing that the number of posts earmarked for deputation in the cadres of the CAPFs up to the level of SAG should be progressively reduced over a period of time, say within an upper limit of two years.”

In an affidavit, the Union Home Secretary had informed the court that 46 IPS officers have been brought on deputation to the CAPFs up to the SAG level after the court’s 2025 judgment.

Two weeks time

The court has directed the Home Secretary to file an affidavit within two weeks detailing the procedure followed for bringing the officers on deputation.

According to the affidavit, the Border Security Force (BSF) received 13 IPS officers, Central Industrial Security Force (CISF) 11, the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) nine, the Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) six and Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB) seven officers.

To circumvent the 2025 judgment, the government enacted the CAPFs (General Administration) Act, 2026 that was published in the gazette on April 9. However, seven writ petitions challenging the legislation have since been filed and are scheduled for hearing before the Supreme Court on November 18.

The Act, passed by Parliament on April 2, states that in all CAPFs, 50% of the total posts in the rank of Inspector General, at least 67% posts in the rank of Additional Director General and all posts in the rank of Special Director General and Director General shall be filled by IPS officers on deputation. Until now, such postings were done based on executive orders. The 50% cap on DIG posts, to be filled by Group A CAPF officers, was also done away with, paving the way for higher percentage of IPS deputation.

title: Javelin | An icon of modern warfare
author: Murali N. Krishnaswamy
content_html:
“BIG news! India plans to buy the battle-tested Javelin anti-tank system”, U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor posted on X on August 28. This is “a great step forward in the U.S.-India defense relationship, opening the door to co-production possibilities”, he wrote. The significance of the announcement lies not merely in the planned purchase, but in what the Javelin brings to India’s defence arsenal.

Developed and made by the Javelin Joint Venture (JJV) between Raytheon and Lockheed Martin, the Javelin has been described as a versatile, portable and multi-purpose weapon system that can handle a spectrum of threats. More precisely, it is a ‘fire-and-forget’ anti-tank guided missile (ATGM) system that comprises a Command Launch Unit (CLU) and the missile. The CLU has the day/night sighting system, the electronics and the controls while the missile’s imaging infrared seeker guides it after the launch. Locking onto its target before launch, it allows the operator to move away after firing.

A peek into the company’s production literature uncovers the following list: with over 20 years of performance, the Javelin has been in action in operations across a range of theatres. After classroom training of only 72 hours, a soldier can take advantage of the missile’s ‘low-signature’ launch (or minimal detectability) to carry out a variety of attack modes; these range from top-attack targets such as tanks to direct-attack capability for caves, bunkers or soft targets.

Operational readiness

And, with an operational readiness rate of 99% and an engagement success rate of 94%, the armament has established itself as a mainstay brigade combat team weapon for the U.S. Army and U.S. Marine Corps. It is expected to be in the U.S. military’s operational inventory until 2050. The company has also highlighted its economic impact, covering 63 domestic suppliers in 18 states and 22 international suppliers. But it is one point that stands out: the detail of “5,000 combat firings (Prior to Ukraine)”.

In service since 1996, the Javelin has been used in the invasion of Iraq in 2003 and also in Afghanistan. Yet, it is in Ukraine that the Javelin acquired its reputation as a weapon that could take on Russian might. The Javelin also has an interesting imagery. In a 2022 article, journalist Matthew Gault, who writes on conflict and culture, highlighted the popularity of “St. Javelin, a symbol of the conflict in Ukraine”. Surrounded by a bright red halo and the golden trident coat-of-arms of Ukraine, this creation of ‘meme-mythology’, clad in green robes, carries an FGM-148 Javelin anti-tank missile launcher in her arms, portraying a defiant symbol of resistance.

For India, the nitty-gritty of the August 2026 announcement lies in the proposed assembly of the ATGMs; in the memorandum of understanding between JJV and Tata Advanced Systems Ltd (TASL), Javelin All Up Rounds (AURs) are to be co-produced domestically. Much of the component production would be in the U.S. where the Lockheed Martin plant in Alabama will produce the Javelin’s “sub-assembly kits”, while Raytheon’s facility in Arizona will manufacture its “guidance electronics units”. Both systems will then be shipped to TASL for final assembly and incorporation into the ATGM. In essence, the U.S. will hold the reins.

The development also marks the difficulty that India has faced in overcoming a hurdle: it has taken it over 15 years to resolve differences with the U.S. over technology transfer and local production. During this time, India has maintained a diverse anti-tank inventory, including limited supplies of the Israeli Spike, while pursuing the Defence Research and Development Organisation’s ‘Third Generation’ Fire and Forget Man Portable Anti-Tank Guided Missile.

However, to a few established defence commentators, such as Rahul Bedi, the subtext of Mr. Gor’s “big news” is the path that India has chosen for its anti-tank missile programme — either as a looming shadow over its indigenous missile efforts or a pragmatic response to a pressing military requirement.

title: Eight High Court judges appointed as Chief Justices
author: Ishita Mishra
content_html:
President Droupadi Murmu on Saturday (September 5, 2026) appointed eight judges of various High Courts as Chief Justices of different High Courts.

Law and justice Minister Arjunram Meghwal, who took to social media platform X, making an announcement regarding the appointments, said the same were done by the President in exercise of the power conferred by the Constitution of India and in consultation with the Chief Justice of India.

According to the appointments notified on Saturday, Justice Sanjay Kumar Agarwal of the Chhattisgarh High Court has been appointed Chief Justice of the Rajasthan High Court. His appointment comes amid a recent controversy involving Acting Chief Justice Sanjeev Prakash Sharma. The controversy became public after Supreme Court judge Justice Sandeep Mehta wrote to Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant, raising concerns about Justice Sharma’s conduct.

The allegations triggered protests by lawyers in Rajasthan. Justice Sharma has denied the charges, calling them baseless and stating that he has submitted his response to the CJI.

Also, Justice Valluri Kameswar Rao of the Delhi High Court has been appointed Chief Justice of the Patna High Court, while Justice Ravindra V. Ghuge of the Bombay High Court will head the Calcutta High Court.

Justice Ashwani Kumar Mishra of the Punjab and Haryana High Court has been appointed Chief Justice of the same court.

Justice Krushna Ram Mohapatra of the Orissa High Court has been appointed Chief Justice of the Chhattisgarh High Court, while Justice Alpesh Yeshwant Kogje of the Gujarat High Court will head the Madhya Pradesh High Court.

Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi of the Allahabad High Court will take over as Chief Justice of the Bombay High Court.

Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati of the Rajasthan High Court has been appointed Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.

title: VTU asks principals of engineering colleges to dedicate time slots for student interaction and grievance redressal
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
The Visvesvaraya Technological University (VTU) has issued a circular instructing principals of affiliated engineering colleges to dedicate time slots for student interaction and grievance redressal.

“Principals are asked to earmark and clearly display specific time slots during which students may meet the principal for discussion of their academic, administrative, or other genuine grievances. The designated time for student interaction shall be prominently displayed outside the principal’s chamber, so that students are aware of the appropriate time,” it is stated.

The colleges have been asked to maintain a grievance log book. In the log book, the principal must record the date, brief nature of the grievance/query, and the action taken or resolution provided, wherever applicable.

Meanwhile, VTU has informed the colleges that the availability and implementation of such a system may also be verified by the Local Inspection Committee (LIC) during the affiliation/inspection process.

title: Spotlight on illegal coal trade in Meghalaya after truck accident
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
A road accident involving a coal-laden truck has reignited the debate on illegal mining and transportation of the fossil fuel in Meghalaya.

The National Green Tribunal (NGT) banned hazardous rat-hole coal mining in the State in April 2014. The Supreme Court upheld the ban while allowing scientific mining under strict statutory compliance.

However, a series of disasters and associated deaths have pointed to rampant illegal coal mining.

In its 40th Interim Report submitted to the High Court of Meghalaya recently, the Justice (retired) B.P. Katakey Committee sought a detailed inquiry into whether the coal transported in a truck involved in an accident near Meghalaya’s capital, Shillong, on the morning of August 24 was legally auctioned or illegally mined.

The NGT and the apex court had allowed Coal India Limited to auction coal that was mined and stocked before the 2014 ban.

The committee, appointed by the High Court, called for a probe after finding that the vehicle lacked the mandatory Mineral Transport Challan issued by the Directorate of Mineral Resources.

According to the State Police, the truck that overturned was being driven from Nongstoin in Meghalaya’s West Khasi Hills district toward Assam’s Guwahati. The truck operator appeared before the police station concerned and produced documents, claiming that the coal was auctioned and belonged to a successful bidder for 8,338.374 metric tonnes.

The operator also produced a photocopy of a Mineral Transport Challan for another truck, claiming that it had to be replaced by another (the one that met with the accident) following a breakdown, the police said. The operator, however, could not produce the original challan for either truck.

According to the committee, this violated the Standard Operating Procedure governing the transportation of auctioned coal. It called for a probe to establish the origin of the transported coal and asked the police to submit a status report within a fortnight from September 4. 

The panel further sought to know why the authorities have not undertaken the confiscation process despite seizing 92 items of equipment and 62 vehicles, in cases related to illegal coal trade registered between 2023 and August 2026.

Information furnished by the Meghalaya Police revealed that 64 cases relating to illegal transportation and 127 cases relating to illegal extraction of coal were registered across the State during these four years.

The committee also flagged the lack of action against landowners and mine owners, except for four cases in East Jaintia Hills district.

title: MLA seeks steps to address water shortage in Chittoor, Vaduthala areas
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
Ernakulam MLA T.J. Vinod has written to Water Resources Minister Mons Joseph seeking immediate action to address drinking water shortage in Chittoor area of ​​Cheranalloor grama panchayat and Vaduthala area of ​​the Kochi Corporation.

Drinking water supply in Chittoor and Vaduthala areas has been significantly disrupted for nearly a month, causing immense difficulty to residents, the MLA said in the letter.

Mr. Vinod urged the Minister to issue necessary instructions to officials to resolve the issue.
